snip.t: Infectious & Immune-mediated: Advanced HIV causes direct myocyte toxicity, cytokine-driven apoptosis, or secondary myocarditis via opportunistic pathogens (e.g., cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis).
Depressed GCS, focal deficits, or seizures signal cerebral malaria, bacterial meningitis, or intracranial tuberculoma/toxoplasmosis.
These indicate central nervous system (CNS) infections like cryptococcal meningitis, cerebral toxoplasmosis, or tuberculoma.

*Stage 4:* Severe symptoms (defining illnesses); HIV wasting syndrome, PCP, extrapulmonary TB, cryptococcal meningitis, cerebral toxoplasmosis, Kaposi sarcoma, CMV retinitis, and chronic herpes simplex ulcerations.
Crucial for CNS infections (e.g., Cryptococcal meningitis, cerebral toxoplasmosis, neurocysticercosis, cerebral malaria).
Exposure history: Contact with soil, bird/bat droppings, contaminated water/food, animals (cats for toxoplasmosis).
Depending on the clinical context, malaria, rubella, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, herpes simplex and other infections may also be relevant.

qs.q: A young female patient presents with posterior triangle lymphadenopathy and is diagnosed with toxoplasmosis. What crucial lifestyle or medical counseling must be provided regarding her management?
qs.e: Management of toxoplasmosis includes supportive treatment and advising the patient to avoid pregnancy until the infection is cleared due to teratogenic risks. Dietary sodium restriction is irrelevant to this protozoal infection.

qs.q: During lifestyle counseling for preconception care, a healthcare provider advises a patient regarding dietary safety to avoid specific food-borne infections like toxoplasmosis and listeria. Which specific dietary habit should be avoided?
o: Consuming fresh citrus fruits in the daily diet
Drinking pasteurized milk as a beverage option
Eating thoroughly cooked fish in the diet plan
Consuming raw meat in the daily food intake
qs.e: Avoiding raw meat is essential during preconception and pregnancy to prevent toxoplasmosis and listeria infections. Thoroughly cooked foods and pasteurized products do not carry the same risk.

ai.title: Toxoplasmosis (Cerebral and Systemic)
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Toxoplasma gondii infection can be asymptomatic or cause severe disease, especially in immunocompromised patients. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on clinical clues and limited labs, and treatment must balance efficacy with drug availability.

sections.p: Toxoplasmosis is infection with the intracellular protozoan Toxoplasma gondii. Diagnosis combines exposure history, clinical syndrome, and laboratory testing.
b: Serology (IgG/IgM) indicates past or recent infection.
PCR on CSF or blood detects active parasite DNA.
Imaging (CT/MRI) shows ring‑enhancing lesions in the brain.

t.b: Has the patient been infected recently? Positive IgM or rising IgG titre suggests recent infection; isolated IgG indicates past exposure.
Is there active parasite replication? Positive PCR confirms active disease, especially useful in HIV patients with CNS lesions.
What is the pattern of CNS involvement? Multiple ring‑enhancing lesions, especially in basal ganglia, support cerebral toxoplasmosis.

sections.p: Severity is judged by organ involvement and host immunity. In HIV, WHO stage 4 includes cerebral toxoplasmosis.
b: Mild: isolated lymphadenopathy or flu‑like illness.
Moderate: ocular disease, myocarditis, or isolated pulmonary infiltrates.
Severe: encephalitis, diffuse CNS lesions, or multi‑organ failure.

sections.p: Transmission routes most relevant in East Africa:
b: Ingestion of oocysts from cat feces contaminating soil or water.
Consumption of undercooked meat (goat, pork, game).
Congenital transmission from an infected mother.
Reactivation in immunosuppressed hosts (advanced HIV, steroids).

sections.p: Presentation varies with immune status and organ involved.
b: Immunocompetent: asymptomatic or mild fever, lymphadenopathy, myalgia.
Ocular: unilateral blurred vision, floaters, vitritis, retinal necrosis.
Cerebral: headache, fever, focal neurological deficits, seizures, altered mental status.
Systemic: pneumonitis, myocarditis, hepatitis, generalized lymphadenopathy.

sections.p: Prioritise tests that change management and are feasible locally.

t.b: Is there a leukocytosis or lymphopenia? May support systemic infection or HIV‑related immunosuppression.
Has the patient been recently infected? Guides need for acute‑phase therapy.
Are there ring‑enhancing lesions? Distinguishes cerebral toxoplasmosis from tuberculoma or lymphoma.
Is parasite DNA present? Confirms active CNS disease.

sections.p: Identify patients who need urgent care.
b: Severe headache with focal deficit or seizures – risk of raised intracranial pressure.
Rapid visual loss – ocular involvement threatening sight.
Cardiac arrhythmia or heart failure – possible myocarditis.
Pregnancy with primary infection – risk of congenital disease.

sections.p: Treat active disease, then provide secondary prophylaxis in immunocompromised hosts.
b: First‑line: Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid (leucovorin) – blocks folate pathway, synergistic parasite kill.
If sulfadiazine unavailable: Pyrimethamine + clindamycin – similar efficacy, avoids sulfonamide allergy.
Adjunctive steroids for severe cerebral edema only if life‑threatening.
Supportive care: control seizures, manage intracranial pressure, treat co‑existing HIV (start/optimise ART).

sections.p: Monitor clinical response and serology; prevent re‑infection and reactivation.
b: Re‑evaluate neurologic status weekly; repeat imaging after 2–3 weeks if no improvement.
In HIV, secondary prophylaxis (pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine) until CD4 >200 cells/µL for >6 months on ART.
Educate on hand‑washing, cooking meat thoroughly, and avoiding cat litter exposure.
Pregnant women: screen seronegative mothers and advise avoidance of raw meat and cat feces.
Cerebral tuberculoma – usually solitary, may have calcification; TB history important.
Primary CNS lymphoma – often solitary, periventricular, CD4 <50 cells/µL; EBV PCR helpful.
Neurocysticercosis – multiple lesions at different stages, often in cortex; history of pork ingestion.
IgM may persist for months, leading to false assumption of acute infection.
Negative serology in immunocompromised patients does not rule out disease.
Ring‑enhancing lesions on CT can be tuberculoma; PCR helps differentiate.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of consciousness, severe seizures, or signs of raised intracranial pressure.
Signs of heart failure or arrhythmia.

faq.q: Why is pyrimethamine combined with sulfadiazine?
faq.a: Pyrimethamine blocks parasite dihydrofolate reductase; sulfadiazine adds a sulfonamide that inhibits folate synthesis, giving synergistic kill.

faq.q: Can a negative IgM rule out cerebral toxoplasmosis in HIV?
faq.a: No; immunosuppressed patients may not mount an IgM response, so imaging and PCR are more reliable.

faq.q: What is the main preventive measure for pregnant women?
faq.a: Avoid raw/undercooked meat and cat litter; screen seronegative mothers early in pregnancy.

exam: A 35‑year‑old HIV patient presents with new seizures and multiple ring‑enhancing lesions on CT – what is your next step? — Start empiric pyrimethamine‑sulfadiazine while arranging PCR; do not wait for definitive diagnosis.

How does cerebral toxoplasmosis differ from tuberculoma on imaging? — Toxoplasmosis usually has multiple lesions, often in basal ganglia, with surrounding edema; tuberculoma often solitary with calcified centre.
Why is folinic acid given with pyrimethamine? — To rescue host bone‑marrow folate metabolism and prevent severe pancytopenia.

A pregnant woman with primary infection is concerned about the fetus – what advice do you give? — Counsel on risk of congenital disease, consider spiramycin if early gestation, and monitor fetal ultrasound for hydrocephalus.
In a resource‑limited hospital without MRI, how would you confirm cerebral toxoplasmosis? — Use CT findings, serology, and clinical risk (HIV CD4 <100); start empiric therapy if compatible.
What are the red‑flag signs that require urgent referral? — Altered consciousness, focal deficits worsening rapidly, severe visual loss, cardiac instability.
Why might sulfadiazine be avoided in a patient with sulfa allergy? — It can cause severe hypersensitivity; clindamycin is the alternative.

Explain the role of ART in preventing toxoplasmosis reactivation. — Effective ART raises CD4 counts, reducing opportunistic reactivation; secondary prophylaxis can be stopped once immune recovery is sustained.
